title: Another Person’s Child
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: O'Brien argues that the most repeated instruction in education, build relationships, has never been defined, and that teachers pay the price. A teacher-student relationship is not friendship, parenting, professional collegiality or therapy; it is a sustained relationship with another person's child, in a compulsory setting, across a power imbalance. Undefined, the instruction collapses into being liked, which makes hard correction harder. He proposes accuracy, ambition and consistency, points to the warm demander, and admits he gave the unfalsifiable advice himself for years.
points: Build relationships is an undefined instruction, and the cost of that imprecision is borne by teachers.
The teacher-student bond is its own category: it is not friendship, parenting, collegiality or therapy.
Without a definition, relationship-building collapses into likability, which makes it harder to deliver hard corrections.
What students need is accuracy, ambition and consistency from the adult, not affection.
Telling a struggling teacher to build a better relationship is unfalsifiable and turns a technique problem into a caring problem.
quotes: I’m not arguing with the premise. I’m arguing that we have never defined it, and that the entire cost of not defining it gets paid by teachers.
It is a sustained relationship with another person’s child, in a compulsory setting, across a real power imbalance, for a fixed period, in service of an outcome he did not choose.

But an undefined instruction collapses into the nearest available behavior, and the nearest available behavior is rapport. Rapport collapses into likability, and likability has one enormous advantage over the real thing: you can feel it.
Not affection. Accuracy plus ambition plus consistency, delivered by someone who is not going anywhere.
It’s not that being liked is bad. It’s that a relationship built purely on being liked makes it harder to say the hard thing, not easier.
An instruction that cannot fail is an instruction that transfers every failure to the person receiving it. She doesn’t have a technique problem. She has, apparently, a caring problem.
Warm is not the concession you make so the demand goes down easier. The warmth is what makes the demand survivable, and the demand is what makes the warmth mean anything.
